A carboxylic acid has both a C=O and an O–H group, and both can take part in hydrogen bonding
with water — the O–H donates a hydrogen bond and the carbonyl oxygen accepts one.
Those bonds release enough energy to make up for breaking the water–water bonds, so the acid dissolves.
Formic, acetic, propanoic and butanoic acids are completely miscible with water for this reason.
Solubility falls off sharply from about C5 upward, because the growing non-polar chain cannot
hydrogen bond and increasingly dominates the molecule.
(B) van der Waals forces and (D) London forces are far too weak to explain complete miscibility,
and (C) is simply irrelevant.
∴ because of hydrogen bonding with water.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|50||0|0.s:
Two effects compete in water, and that is the whole point of the question.
Inductive effect — each CH₃ pushes electron density onto nitrogen, making the lone pair more
available and the amine more basic. On this alone the order would be (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > NH₃.
Solvation — once protonated, the cation is stabilised by hydrogen bonds from water to its N–H
bonds. NH₄⁺ has four such bonds, CH₃NH₃⁺ three, (CH₃)₂NH₂⁺ only two. On this alone the order
would be the reverse.
For these three the inductive effect wins, and the observed order in water is
NH₃ < CH₃NH₂ < (CH₃)₂NH
It is only at the third methyl that solvation and steric hindrance overtake induction, which is
why (CH₃)₃N is *less* basic than (CH₃)₂NH in water though more basic in the gas phase.
∴ NH₃ < CH₃NH₂ < (CH₃)₂NH.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|51||0|0.s:
The ether is (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃, tert-butyl methyl ether, and HI cleaves ethers at the C–O bond.
Step 1 — the ether oxygen is protonated: (CH₃)₃C–O⁺(H)–CH₃.
Step 2 — which C–O bond breaks? That depends on which carbocation is available.
The tert-butyl group can form a stable 3° carbocation, so the bond breaks there by SN1:
(CH₃)₃C–O⁺(H)–CH₃ ⇒ (CH₃)₃C⁺ + CH₃OH
Step 3 — iodide attacks the carbocation: (CH₃)₃C⁺ + I⁻ ⇒ (CH₃)₃C–I
So the products are methanol and tert-butyl iodide.
The contrast is worth remembering: if both groups were primary there would be no stable
carbocation, the mechanism would be SN2, and iodide would attack the *less* hindered carbon instead.
∴ CH₃OH + (CH₃)₃C–I.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|52||0|0.s:
Go through the reductions a ketone will undergo.
(A) NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ — hydride reduction of C=O to CH–OH, giving the secondary alcohol ✓
(B) Zn–Hg with concentrated HCl — Clemmensen reduction, taking C=O all the way to CH₂ ✓
(C) Hydrazine with KOH in ethylene glycol — Wolff–Kishner reduction, also C=O to CH₂, used when
the compound cannot survive the acid of a Clemmensen ✓
(D) H₂ with palladium on barium sulphate and quinoline — this is a deliberately *poisoned* catalyst.
Quinoline and BaSO₄ reduce its activity so that it stops after one step. It is used as Lindlar's
catalyst for alkyne ⇒ cis-alkene, and in the Rosenmund reduction of an acid chloride to an aldehyde.
It is not active enough to reduce a ketone.
∴ hydrogen over Pd/BaSO₄ with quinoline cannot do it.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|53||0|0:
Trace the Gabriel synthesis step by step and see which reagent never appears.
Step 1 — phthalimide has an acidic N–H, flanked by two carbonyls. KOH removes that proton to
give potassium phthalimide ⇒ KOH is used.
Step 2 — the phthalimide anion is a nucleophile and displaces halide from an alkyl halide (SN2),
giving N-alkylphthalimide ⇒ alkyl halides are used.
Step 3 — the product is hydrolysed to release the amine, usually with aqueous NaOH, giving the
primary amine and phthalate ⇒ NaOH is used.
HCl plays no part. The method works precisely because no acid is needed; that is what keeps
the product a clean primary amine, free of the secondary and tertiary amines that alkylating
ammonia directly would also produce.
(Note the method fails for aryl amines, since aryl halides will not undergo this SN2 step.)
∴ HCl is not used.
